property: conditional on $x_2$, variable $x_3$ is independent of
variable $x_1$. The joint probability of all the variables shown here is
$p(x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3) =  \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3)
\psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$. Using
$p(a,b) = p(a \bigm | b) p(b)$, we can also write the probability of the
$x$ variables conditioned on the observations $y$,
$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3 \bigm | y_1, y_2, y_3) =  
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3).$$
For brevity, we write $p(\mathbf{y})$ for $p(y_1, y_2, y_3)$. Thus, to
form the conditional distribution, within a normalization factor, we
simply include the observed variable values into the joint probability.
For vision applications, we often use such Markov chain structures to
describe events over time.

To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a **Markov random field** (MRF) @Blake2011:

![Two-dimensional Markov random field.](figures/graphical_models/mrf.png){width="48%" #fig-leafs}

Then the joint probability over all the variables factorizes into this
product: 

$$p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) = 
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})}
\prod_{(i,j)} \phi_{ij}(x_i, x_j) \prod_i \psi_i(x_i, y_i),$$
where the first product is over all spatial neighbors $i$ and $j$, and the second
product is over all nodes $i$.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in @fig-leafs, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (@fig-leafs [a]). @fig-leafs [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

:::{#fig-leafs layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/graphical_models/leaf2.jpg){width=97% #fig-leafs-a}

![](figures/graphical_models/leaf1.jpg){width=100% #fig-leafs-b}

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red.  (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.
::: 

## Directed Graphical Models

In addition to undirected graphical models, another type of graphical
model is commonly used. **Directed graphical models** @Koller2009
describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of
conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph
contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the
probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating
arrows pointing into it. So this graph

![A directed graphical model with three variables.](figures/graphical_models/directed.png){width="20%" #eq-directedjoint}

denotes the joint probability,

elements: 3x3 horizontal grid of hidden nodes (spheres, labeled x_ij)
3x3 elevated grid of observation nodes (spheres, labeled y_ij directly above each x_ij)
Horizontal and diagonal undirected grid edges connecting the hidden x_ij nodes in a 2D lattice
Vertical undirected edges connecting each hidden x_ij node to its corresponding observation y_ij node
Text labels: x1, x2, x3 and y1, y2, y3 for the back row of nodes
Color/shading of observation nodes (representing noisy pixel inputs, e.g., red/blue mixture)
Color/shading of hidden nodes (representing denoised segment labels, dynamically updated)
Highlighted halo/pulses around active edges/nodes to represent local potentials (phi and psi)

interactions.label: Spatial Coupling (phi)
interactions.teaches: Higher spatial coupling (phi) forces neighboring hidden nodes to agree on their state, smoothing out noise and forming coherent segment regions.

interactions.label: Observation Noise
interactions.teaches: Simulates noise in the observed pixel values (y). Denoising relies on the spatial coupling to reconstruct the true underlying segment layout.

demo_steps.title: The MRF architecture
demo_steps.narration: This 2D Markov Random Field represents an image grid. The top layer contains observed pixels (y), while the bottom layer contains hidden, clean segment labels (x). Each hidden node is connected to its observation vertically (psi potential) and its spatial neighbors horizontally (phi potential).

demo_steps.title: Noisy observations
demo_steps.narration: When observation noise increases, the input layer (y) becomes a chaotic mix of colors. If spatial coupling is weak, the hidden layer (x) blindly trusts the noisy data, resulting in a fragmented, highly inaccurate segmentation.

demo_steps.title: Spatial smoothing (Denoising)
demo_steps.narration: By increasing the spatial coupling (phi), we encourage neighboring pixels to share the same segment label. The MRF filters out the high-frequency noise, recovering a clean, contiguous boundary (like the segmented leaf in the textbook).

demo_steps.title: Interactive inference
demo_steps.narration: Click on any hidden node to see its local dependencies. Its final state is a mathematical compromise between its vertical data likelihood (psi) and its horizontal neighbor agreements (phi).

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: An elevated, isometric-style perspective looking down onto the 3D double-layer grid from the front-left, clearly separating the top observation layer from the bottom hidden layer.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant structural plane is the horizontal 2D grid of nodes, which recedes diagonally from bottom-left to upper-right. (2) This receding diagonal indicates an azimuth angle that is offset from the cardinal directions; an azimuth around -35 degrees properly captures this diagonal projection without collapsing the columns. (3) The vertical offset of the 'y' nodes above 'x' implies we need a moderately shallow elevation (around 25 degrees) to clearly see the vertical 'stalk' connections without the top nodes completely overlapping and obscuring the bottom nodes.

camera_view.view_notes: Matches the classic 3D network diagram layout: rows go from left to right, cols go from front to back, and observations are elevated vertically above the grid.

interactionPlan.notes: Nodes should be rendered as shiny spheres. The observation nodes (top layer) should have a slightly darker, metallic, or textured appearance. The hidden nodes (bottom layer) should change color dynamically based on the slider values (e.g., using a simple simulated annealing or mean-field approximation to update their colors in real-time as noise and coupling parameters change). Clicking a node should trigger a glowing shader effect on its connected edges.
